questions.question: A system matrix is given as follows \[A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & -1 \\ -6 & -11 & 6 \\ -6 & -11 & 5 \end{bmatrix} .\] The absolute value of the ratio of the maximum eigenvalue to the minimum eigenvalue is ________
questions.explanation:
The characteristic equation of the system matrix \(A\) is determined by finding the roots of its characteristic determinant: \[|A - \lambda I| = 0\] \[\begin{vmatrix} -\lambda & 1 & -1 \\ -6 & -11 - \lambda & 6 \\ -6 & -11 & 5 - \lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0\] \[(-\lambda) \left[(-11 - \lambda)(5 - \lambda) - (6)(-11)\right] - 1 \left[(-6)(5 - \lambda) - (6)(-6)\right] + (-1) \left[(-6)(-11) - (-11 - \lambda)(-6)\right] = 0\] \[\begin{gathered}
    (-\lambda) \left[\lambda^2 + 6\lambda - 55 + 66\right] - 1 \left[-30 + 6\lambda + 36\right] - 1 \left[66 - (66 + 6\lambda)\right] = 0 \\
    (-\lambda) \left[\lambda^2 + 6\lambda + 11\right] - 1 \left[6\lambda + 6\right] - 1 \left[-6\lambda\right] = 0 \\
    -\lambda^3 - 6\lambda^2 - 11\lambda - 6\lambda - 6 + 6\lambda = 0 \\
    -\lambda^3 - 6\lambda^2 - 11\lambda - 6 = 0
\end{gathered}\] \[\lambda^3 + 6\lambda^2 + 11\lambda + 6 = 0\] By inspection or using the rational root theorem, we find that \(\lambda = -1\) is a root because \((-1)^3 + 6(-1)^2 + 11(-1) + 6 = -1 + 6 - 11 + 6 = 0\). Factoring out \((\lambda + 1)\) via polynomial long division: \[(\lambda + 1)(\lambda^2 + 5\lambda + 6) = 0 \implies (\lambda + 1)(\lambda + 2)(\lambda + 3) = 0\] Thus, the distinct eigenvalues of matrix \(A\) are: \[\lambda = -1, -2, -3\] Evaluating the absolute ratio yields: \[\text{Required Ratio} = \left| \frac{\lambda_{\text{max}}}{\lambda_{\text{min}}} \right| = \frac{|-1|}{|-3|} = \frac{1}{3} = \boxed{0.33}\]

questions.question: Two matrices \(A\) and \(B\) are given below: \[A = \begin{bmatrix} p & q \\ r & s \end{bmatrix}; \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix} p^2 + q^2 & pr + qs \\ pr + qs & r^2 + s^2 \end{bmatrix}\] If the rank of matrix \(A\) is \(N\), then the rank of matrix \(B\) is
questions.explanation:
Given the two real square matrices \(A\) and \(B\): \[A = \begin{bmatrix} p & q \\ r & s \end{bmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix} p^2 + q^2 & pr + qs \\ pr + qs & r^2 + s^2 \end{bmatrix}\]
Method 1
Let us evaluate the determinant of matrix \(A\) and \(B\): \[|A| = ps - qr\] \[|B| = \left(p^2 + q^2\right)\left(r^2 + s^2\right) - (pr + qs)^2\] \[|B| = \left(p^2r^2 + p^2s^2 + q^2r^2 + q^2s^2\right) - \left(p^2r^2 + q^2s^2 + 2pqrs\right)\] \[|B| = p^2s^2 + q^2r^2 - 2pqrs\] \[|B| = (ps - qr)^2\] \[|B| = |A|^2\]
  • If \(|A| \neq 0\), then matrix \(A\) is non-singular and has full rank, so \(\rho(A) = 2\). Since \(|B| = |A|^2 \neq 0\), matrix \(B\) is also non-singular and has full rank, so \(\rho(B) = 2\).
  • If \(|A| = 0\), then \(\rho(A) < 2\). Since \(|B| = |A|^2 = 0\), \(\rho(B) < 2\). For non-zero elements, the rank reduces identically based on structural linear dependency.
Therefore, if the rank of matrix \(A\) is \(N\) (\(\rho(A) = N\)), the rank of matrix \(B\) is also \(N\) (\(\rho(B) = N\)). \[\boxed{\text{(C) N}}\]
Method 2
We can alternatively solve this using matrix multiplication properties. Let us observe the product of matrix \(A\) with its transpose \(A^{\top}\): \[A = \begin{bmatrix} p & q \\ r & s \end{bmatrix} \implies A^{\top} = \begin{bmatrix} p & r \\ q & s \end{bmatrix}\] \[A A^{\top} = \begin{bmatrix} p & q \\ r & s \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} p & r \\ q & s \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} p(p) + q(q) & p(r) + q(s) \\ r(p) + s(q) & r(r) + s(s) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} p^2 + q^2 & pr + qs \\ pr + qs & r^2 + s^2 \end{bmatrix}\] \[B = A A^{\top}\] By applying the fundamental properties of matrix rank, we know that for any real matrix \(A\): \[\rho(B) = \rho(A A^{\top}) = \rho(A)\] Thus, if \(\rho(A) = N\), then \(\rho(B) = N\).
\[\boxed{\text{(C) N}}\]
Key points
  • Rank Product Property: For any real matrix \(A\), the rank of \(A\) is identical to the rank of its gram matrix product: \(\rho(A) = \rho(A^{\top}) = \rho(A A^{\top}) = \rho(A^{\top} A)\).
  • Determinant Product Rule: \(\det(AB) = \det(A)\det(B)\). Since \(\det(A^{\top}) = \det(A)\), it directly follows that \(\det(A A^{\top}) = \det(A)^2\).

questions.question: Let \(f(x) = xe^{-x}\). The maximum value of the function in the interval \((0, \infty)\) is
questions.explanation: Given the function: \[f(x) = xe^{-x}\] We need to find the maximum value of \(f(x)\) in the open interval \((0, \infty)\). To locate the stationary points, we differentiate \(f(x)\) with respect to \(x\) using the product rule: \[f'(x) = \frac{d}{dx}(x) \cdot e^{-x} + x \cdot \frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{-x}\right)\] \[f'(x) = 1 \cdot e^{-x} + x \cdot \left(-e^{-x}\right)\] \[f'(x) = (1 - x)e^{-x}\] Setting the first derivative to zero for stationary points: \[f'(x) = 0\] \[(1 - x)e^{-x} = 0\] Since \(e^{-x} \neq 0\) for any real value of \(x\), we have: \[1 - x = 0 \implies x = 1\] The stationary point \(x = 1\) lies within the given interval \((0, \infty)\). To confirm whether this point yields a maximum, we find the second derivative \(f''(x)\): \[f''(x) = \frac{d}{dx}\left[(1 - x)e^{-x}\right]\] \[f''(x) = (-1)e^{-x} + (1 - x)\left(-e^{-x}\right)\] \[f''(x) = -e^{-x} - e^{-x} + xe^{-x}\] \[f''(x) = (x - 2)e^{-x}\] Evaluating the second derivative at the stationary point \(x = 1\): \[f''(1) = (1 - 2)e^{-1} = -e^{-1} = -\frac{1}{e}\] Since \(f''(1) < 0\), the function attains a local maximum at \(x = 1\). Now, calculating the maximum value of the function: \[f_{\text{max}} = f(1) = 1 \cdot e^{-1} = e^{-1}\] \[\boxed{\text{(a) } e^{-1} }\]

questions.question: To evaluate the double integral \(\int_{0}^{8} \left( \int_{y/2}^{(y/2)+1} \left( \dfrac{2x - y}{2} \right) dx \right) dy\), we make the substitution \(u = \left( \dfrac{2x - y}{2} \right)\) and \(v = \dfrac{y}{2}\). The integral will reduce to
questions.explanation:
We need to evaluate the given double integral using change of variables: \[I = \int_{0}^{8} \left( \int_{y/2}^{(y/2)+1} \left(\frac{2x - y}{2}\right) dx \right) dy\] The given transformations are: \[u = \frac{2x - y}{2} = x - \frac{y}{2}\] \[v = \frac{y}{2} \implies y = 2v\] Substituting \(y = 2v\) into the expression for \(u\): \[u = x - v \implies x = u + v\] Next, we compute the Jacobian matrix of transformation \(J\): \[J = \frac{\partial(x, y)}{\partial(u, v)} = \begin{vmatrix} \frac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \frac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \frac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix}\] Computing the partial derivatives: \[\frac{\partial x}{\partial u} = 1, \quad \frac{\partial x}{\partial v} = 1\] \[\frac{\partial y}{\partial u} = 0, \quad \frac{\partial y}{\partial v} = 2\] Therefore, the Jacobian determinant is: \[J = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = (1 \times 2) - (1 \times 0) = 2\] Now, let us transform the limits of integration:
  • For the inner limits (\(x\) as a function of \(y\)):
    • Lower limit: \(x = \frac{y}{2}\) \[u = \left(\frac{y}{2}\right) - \frac{y}{2} = 0\]
    • Upper limit: \(x = \frac{y}{2} + 1\) \[u = \left(\frac{y}{2} + 1\right) - \frac{y}{2} = 1\]
  • For the outer limits (\(y\)):
    • Lower limit: \(y = 0 \implies v = \frac{0}{2} = 0\)
    • Upper limit: \(y = 8 \implies v = \frac{8}{2} = 4\)
Using the transformation formula \(\iint_{R} f(x,y) \,dx\,dy = \iint_{R'} f(x(u,v), y(u,v)) \cdot |J| \,du\,dv\): \[I = \int_{0}^{4} \left( \int_{0}^{1} u \cdot 2 \,du \right) dv\] \[I = \int_{0}^{4} \left( \int_{0}^{1} 2u \,du \right) dv\] \[\boxed{\text{(b) } \int_{0}^{4} \left(\int_{0}^{1} 2u\,du\right) dv}\]

questions.question: The minimum value of the function \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 24x + 100\) in the interval \([-3, 3]\) is
questions.explanation:
Given the function: \[f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 24x + 100\] We need to find the minimum value of \(f(x)\) in the closed interval \([-3, 3]\). First, find the stationary points by setting the first derivative to zero: \[f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x - 24\] \[3x^2 - 6x - 24 = 0\] \[x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0\] \[(x - 4)(x + 2) = 0 \implies x = 4 \text{ or } x = -2\] Let's check which stationary points lie within our interval \([-3, 3]\):
  • \(x = -2 \in [-3, 3]\) (Valid critical point)
  • \(x = 4 \notin [-3, 3]\) (Ignore since it lies outside the interval)
To check the nature of the critical point at \(x = -2\), we compute the second derivative: \[f''(x) = 6x - 6\] \[f''(-2) = 6(-2) - 6 = -18 < 0\] Since \(f''(-2) < 0\), \(x = -2\) is a point of local maximum. The global minimum over a closed interval must occur either at the boundaries of the interval or at a local minimum point inside the interval. Since there is no local minimum inside \([-3, 3]\), the global minimum must occur at one of the endpoints, \(x = -3\) or \(x = 3\). Evaluating \(f(x)\) at the boundaries:
  • At \(x = -3\): \[f(-3) = (-3)^3 - 3(-3)^2 - 24(-3) + 100\] \[f(-3) = -27 - 27 + 72 + 100 = 118\]
  • At \(x = 3\): \[f(3) = (3)^3 - 3(3)^2 - 24(3) + 100\] \[f(3) = 27 - 27 - 72 + 100 = 28\]
Comparing the boundary values: \[\text{Global minimum} = \min\{f(-3), f(3)\} = \min\{118, 28\} = 28\] \[\boxed{\text{(b) } 28}\]

questions.question: A particle, starting from origin at \(t = 0\text{ s}\), is traveling along \(x-\text{axis}\) with velocity \[v = \frac{\pi}{2} \cos\left( \frac{\pi}{2} t \right)\text{ m/s}\] At \(t = 3\text{ s}\), the difference between the distance covered by the particle and the magnitude of displacement from the origin is ________.
questions.explanation:
Given the velocity of the particle along the \(x\)-axis: \[v(t) = \frac{\pi}{2} \cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{2}\right)\] The particle starts from the origin at \(t = 0\,\text{s}\), so the initial position is \(x(0) = 0\). The position \(x(t)\) (displacement from the origin) is given by the integral of velocity: \[x(t) = \int v(t) \,dt = \int \frac{\pi}{2} \cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{2}\right) \,dt\] \[x(t) = \frac{\pi}{2} \cdot \frac{\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{2}\right)}{\frac{\pi}{2}} + c = \sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{2}\right) + c\] Using the initial condition \(x(0) = 0\): \[0 = \sin(0) + c \implies c = 0\] \[x(t) = \sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{2}\right)\] 1. Finding the Magnitude of Displacement at \(t = 3\,\text{s}\): \[x(3) = \sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}\right) = -1\,\text{m}\] \[\text{Magnitude of displacement } |\Delta x| = |-1| = 1\,\text{m}\] 2. Finding the Total Distance Covered from \(t = 0\,\text{s}\) to \(t = 3\,\text{s}\): Distance is the integral of speed \(|v(t)|\). Alternatively, because \(x(t) = \sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{2}\right)\) is an oscillating function, we track its motion profile at key time steps where the direction changes (\(v(t) = 0\)):
  • At \(t = 0\,\text{s}\): \(x(0) = 0\,\text{m}\)
  • At \(t = 1\,\text{s}\): \(x(1) = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 1\,\text{m}\) (Particle moves \(1\,\text{m}\) right)
  • At \(t = 2\,\text{s}\): \(x(2) = \sin(\pi) = 0\,\text{m}\) (Particle moves \(1\,\text{m}\) left back to origin)
  • At \(t = 3\,\text{s}\): \(x(3) = \sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}\right) = -1\,\text{m}\) (Particle moves \(1\,\text{m}\) left past origin)
Summing the absolute individual distances traveled in each interval: \[\text{Total Distance} = |1 - 0| + |0 - 1| + |-1 - 0| = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3\,\text{m}\] 3. Finding the Required Difference: \[\text{Difference} = (\text{Total Distance}) - (\text{Magnitude of Displacement})\] \[\text{Difference} = 3 - |-1| = 3 - 1 = 2\] \[\boxed{2}\]

questions.question: The solution for the differential equation \[\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-9x,\] with initial conditions \(x(0)=1\) and \(\left.\dfrac{dx}{dt}\right|_{t=0}=1,\) is
questions.explanation:
The given differential equation is \[\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -9x\ \ \text{with initial conditions}\ \ x(0) = 1,\ \left.\frac{dx}{dt}\right|_{t=0} = 1\]
Method 1
Assume a solution of the form \(x = e^{mt}.\) Substituting into the differential equation, the auxiliary equation is \[m^2e^{mt}+9e^{mt} = 0\] Since \(e^{mt}\neq 0\), \[m^2 + 9 = 0\] \[m = \pm 3j\] For complex roots \(m=\alpha\pm j\beta\), the solution is \[x(t) = e^{\alpha t}\left(C_1\cos\beta t + C_2\sin\beta t\right)\] Here, \(\alpha=0\) and \(\beta=3\), hence \[x(t) = C_1\cos 3t+C_2\sin 3t\] Using \(x(0)=1\), \(1 = C_1\) Therefore, \[x(t) = \cos 3t + C_2\sin 3t\] Differentiating, \[\frac{dx}{dt} = -3\sin 3t + 3C_2\cos 3t\] Using \(\left.\dfrac{dx}{dt}\right|_{t=0}=1,\) \[1 = 3C_2 \Rightarrow\ C_2 = \frac{1}{3}\] Hence, \[x(t) = \cos 3t + \frac{1}{3}\sin 3t.\]
Method 2
Observe that \[\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -9x\] is the equation of a simple harmonic oscillator with angular frequency \(\omega=3.\) The standard solution is \[x(t) = A\cos \omega t + B\sin \omega t\] \[x(t) = A\cos 3t + B\sin 3t\] Using the initial position, \(x(0) = A = 1.\) Differentiating, \[\frac{dx}{dt} = -3A\sin 3t + 3B\cos 3t\] Applying \(\left.\dfrac{dx}{dt}\right|_{t=0} = 1,\) \[3B = 1, \Rightarrow\ B = \frac{1}{3}\] Therefore, \[x(t) = \cos 3t+\frac{1}{3}\sin 3t.\]
\[\boxed{\text{(C)}\ \frac{1}{3}\sin 3t + \cos 3t}\]
Key points
  • The equation \[\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} + \omega^2x = 0\] represents simple harmonic motion (SHM).

questions.question: Consider the differential equation \(x^2\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}+x\dfrac{dy}{dx}-y=0.\) Which of the following is a solution to this differential equation for \(x>0?\)
questions.explanation:
The given differential equation is \[x^2\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + x\frac{dy}{dx} - y = 0\] This is a Cauchy--Euler (or equidimensional) differential equation of the form \[x^2y'' + axy' + by = 0\] We are required to identify a function that satisfies the differential equation. For a Cauchy--Euler equation, assume a trial solution \(y = x^m.\) Substituting into the differential equation, \[x^2\bigl[m(m-1)x^{m-2}\bigr] + x\bigl[mx^{m-1}\bigr] - x^m = 0\] \[m(m-1)x^m + mx^m - x^m = 0\] \[\bigl[m(m-1) + m-1\bigr]x^m = 0\] \[(m^2-1)x^m = 0\] Hence, the auxiliary equation is \[m^2 - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow\ m = \pm 1\] The general solution is \[y = C_1x + C_2x^{-1}\] \[y = C_1x + \frac{C_2}{x}\] Since \(1/x\) is part of the general solution, it satisfies the differential equation. Or verify the options by substituting in the given differential equation. \[\boxed{\text{(C)}\ 1/x}\]
Key points
  • A Cauchy--Euler equation has the standard form \(x^2y''+axy'+by=0.\)
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not use the characteristic equation \(m^2+am+b=0\) meant for constant-coefficient differential equations.

questions.question: All the values of the multi-valued complex function \(1^i\), where \(i = \sqrt{-1}\), are
options: equal in real and imaginary parts.
questions.explanation:
Assume the given expression is: \[x = 1^i\] \[1 = \cos(2n\pi) + i\sin(2n\pi) = e^{i2n\pi}\] \[x = \left(e^{i2n\pi}\right)^i\] \[x = e^{i^2 \cdot 2n\pi}\] \[x = e^{-2n\pi}\] Let us analyze the nature of the resulting values for \(e^{-2n\pi}\):
  • Real values: Since the base \(e\) is a positive real mathematical constant and the exponent \(-2n\pi\) is purely real for any integer \(n\), the value of \(e^{-2n\pi}\) contains no imaginary component. Thus, all values are real.
  • Non-negative values: The exponential function \(e^y\) is strictly positive (\(e^y > 0\)) for any real exponent \(y\). Therefore, \(e^{-2n\pi}\) is always strictly positive, making all values non-negative.
Consequently, all values of \(1^i\) are real and non-negative. \[\boxed{ \text{B. real and non -negative}}\]
Key points
  • Multi-valued Functions: Powers of complex numbers \(z^w\) are generally multi-valued because they depend on the complex logarithm: \(z^w = e^{w \log(z)} = e^{w [\ln|z| + i(\theta + 2n\pi)]}\).
  • Exponential Function Behavior: For any real domain input \(k\), the real-valued function \(f(k) = e^k\) maps entirely onto the strictly positive open interval \((0, \infty)\).
Mistakes to avoid
Do not assume \(1^i = 1\) is the unique solution; ignoring the general argument \(2n\pi\)..

questions.question: Integration of the complex function \(f(z) = \frac{z^2}{z^2 - 1}\), in the counterclockwise direction, around \(|z-1| = 1\), is
questions.explanation:
The given function is: \[f(z) = \frac{z^2}{z^2 - 1} = \frac{z^2}{(z - 1)(z + 1)}\] The singularities of \(f(z)\) are simple poles: \[z^2 - 1 = 0 \implies z = 1, \,-1\] The given contour is a circle described by: \[C : |z - 1| = 1\] This represents a circle centered at \(z = 1\) with a radius of \(1\).
  • For \(z = 1\): \[|1 - 1| = 0 < 1 \implies z = 1 \text{ lies inside the curve } C.\]
  • For \(z = -1\): \[|-1 - 1| = |-2| = 2 > 1 \implies z = -1 \text{ lies outside the curve } C.\]
By Cauchy's Residue Theorem, \[\oint_{C} f(z) \, dz = 2\pi i \, \text{Res}[f(z), 1]\] Residue at the simple pole \(z = 1\): \[\text{Res}[f(z), 1] = \lim_{z \to 1} (z - 1) \frac{z^2}{(z - 1)(z + 1)} = \lim_{z \to 1} \frac{z^2}{z + 1}\] \[\text{Res}[f(z), 1] = \frac{1^2}{1 + 1} = \frac{1}{2}\] \[\oint_{C} f(z) \, dz = 2\pi i \left[ \frac{1}{2} \right] = \pi i\] \[\boxed{C. \pi i}\]

questions.explanation: Let the probability of getting a face with \(n\) dots be proportional to \(n\). Hence, \[P(n)=kn\] where \(k\) is the proportionality constant. Since the total probability is \(1\), \[k(1+2+3+4+5+6)=1\] \[21k=1\] \[k=\frac{1}{21}\] Therefore, the probability of getting the face with three dots is \[P(3)=3k=3\times \frac{1}{21}=\frac{1}{7}\] \[\boxed{0.142}\]

questions.question: A fair coin is tossed \(n\) times. The probability that the difference between the number of heads and tails is \((n-3)\) is
questions.explanation:
Let the number of heads be \(H\) and the number of tails be \(T\). Given, \[H+T=n\] and \[H-T=n-3\] Adding the two equations, \[2H=2n-3\] \[H=\frac{2n-3}{2}\] But the number of heads must be an integer, whereas \[\frac{2n-3}{2}\] is not an integer for any integer \(n\). Hence, such an event is impossible. \[\boxed{\text{(b) }0}\]
Key points
  • In coin toss problems, use: \[H+T=n\]
  • Check whether the obtained values are integers.

questions.question: The function \(f(x) = e^x - 1\) is to be solved using Newton-Raphson method. If the initial value of \(x_0\) is taken 1.0, then the absolute error observed at \(2^{\text{nd}}\) iteration is
questions.explanation:
We want to approximate the root of \(f(x) = e^x - 1 = 0\) using the Newton-Raphson method, starting with an initial guess of \(x_0 = 1.0\). First, calculate the derivative function \(f'(x)\): \[f'(x) = e^x\] The iterative update formula is: \[x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)} = x_n - \dfrac{e^{x_n} - 1}{e^{x_n}} = x_n - 1 + e^{-x_n}\] Let us compute the iterations sequentially: Iteration 1: \[x_1 = x_0 - 1 + e^{-x_0} = 1.0 - 1 + e^{-1} = e^{-1} \approx 0.367879\] Iteration 2:
\[x_2 = x_1 - 1 + e^{-x_1} = 0.367879 - 1 + e^{-0.367879} = -0.632121 + 0.692201 = 0.06008\] The true exact root of the equation \(e^x - 1 = 0\) is \(x_{\text{true}} = 0\). Therefore, the absolute error observed at the second iteration step is: \[\text{Absolute Error} = |x_2 - x_{\text{true}}| = |0.06008 - 0| \approx 0.06\] \[\boxed{0.06}\]
Key points
  • Absolute Error Definition: Absolute numerical error isolates the absolute magnitude deviation between the approximate iterative value and the true exact analytical value: \[\epsilon = |x_{\text{approx}} - x_{\text{true}}|\]

Therefore, \[V_C(0^-)=V_{01}\] Using capacitor voltage continuity, \[V_C(0^+)=V_C(0^-)=V_{01}\] The switch is moved to position \(2\). Again, at steady state the capacitor behaves as an open circuit, so no current flows through the resistor. From the polarity shown, \[V_C(\infty)=-V_{02}\] For a first-order RC circuit, \[V_C(t) = V_f+\left(V_i-V_f\right)e^{-t/\tau}\] where \(V_i\) is the initial capacitor voltage and \(V_f\) is the final capacitor voltage. Substituting, \[V_i=V_{01}, \qquad V_f=-V_{02}\] and \[\tau=2RC\] we get \[V_C(t) = -V_{02} + \left(V_{01}+V_{02}\right)e^{-t/2RC}\] Adding and Subtracting \(V_{01}\) and then rearranging, \[V_C(t) = -\left(V_{01}+V_{02}\right) \left(1-e^{-t/2RC}\right) + V_{01}\] Hence, \[\boxed{ V_C(t) = -\left(V_{01}+V_{02}\right) \left(1-e^{-t/2RC}\right) + V_{01} }\] No options match. {However Gate answer key mentions option D as correct, but it is wrong} Therefore question is MTA.

questions.question: A combination of \(1\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor with an initial voltage \(v_{\text{C}}(0) = -2\text{V}\) in series with a \(100\ \Omega\) resistor is connected to a \(20\text{mA}\) ideal dc current source by operating both switches at \(t = 0\text{ s}\) as shown. Which of the following graphs shown in the options approximates the voltage \(V_{\text{S}}\) across the current source over the next few seconds?
questions.explanation:
At \(t=0\), both switches are operated.
Method Time-Domain Approach
The switch across the current source is opened, forcing the source current \[I_s=20~\text{mA}\] to flow through the resistor-capacitor series circuit. Since capacitor voltage cannot change instantaneously, \[V_C(0^+) = V_C(0^-) = -2~\text{V}\] The resistor voltage at \(t=0^+\) is \[V_R(0^+) = I_sR= 20\times10^{-3}\times100 = 2~\text{V}\] Hence, \[V_s(0^+) = V_C(0^+)+V_R(0^+)\] \[= -2+2 = 0\] For \(t>0\), the current through the capacitor remains constant: \[i_C=I_s\] Using \[i_C=C\frac{dV_C}{dt}\] Integrating, \[V_C(t) = V_C(0^+)+\frac{I_s}{C}t\] \[V_C(t) = -2+\frac{I_s}{C}t\] Therefore, \[V_s(t) = V_C(t)+I_sR\] \[V_s(t) = \left( -2+\frac{I_s}{C}t \right) +I_sR\] Since \[I_sR=2~\text{V}\] \[V_s(t) = \frac{I_s}{C}t\] Thus, \(V_s(t)\) is a straight line passing through the origin with positive slope. Hence, \[\boxed{\textbf{C}}\]
Method Laplace Transform Approach
Using Laplace transforms, \[V_s(s) = \left(\frac{I}{s}\right)\left(\frac{1}{sC}\right) + \left(\frac{I}{s}\right)R + \left(\frac{-2}{s}\right)\] \[V_s(s) = \frac{1}{s} \left( IR-2+\frac{I}{sC} \right)\] Substituting \[I=20\times10^{-3}\text{ A}, \qquad R=100\Omega, \qquad C=1\mu\text{F}\] \[V_s(s) = \frac{1}{s} \left( 20\times10^{-3}\times100 -2 + \frac{20\times10^{-3}} {s\times10^{-6}} \right)\] \[V_s(s) = \frac{1}{s} \left( 2-2+\frac{20\times10^{3}}{s} \right)\] \[V_s(s) = \frac{20\times10^{3}}{s^2} \ \Rightarrow \ V_s(s) = \frac{2\times10^{4}}{s^2}\] Taking inverse Laplace transform, \(\Rightarrow V_s(t) = 2\times10^{4}\,t\,u(t)\) which is the equation of a straight line passing through the origin. Therefore, the correct waveform is \[\boxed{\textbf{C}}\]

questions.question: The voltage across the capacitor, as shown in the figure, is expressed as \[v_c(t)=A_1\sin(\omega_1 t-\theta_1)+A_2\sin(\omega_2 t-\theta_2)\] The values of \(A_1\) and \(A_2\) respectively, are
questions.explanation:
Using superposition theorem, the response is calculated by considering each independent source acting alone. Case 1: Considering the voltage source (open circuit the current source)
The frequency of the voltage source is \(\omega_1 = 10\,\text{rad/s}\). The capacitive reactance is given by: \[X_{C1} = \frac{1}{\omega_1 C} = \frac{1}{10 \times 1} = 0.1\,\Omega\] By potential division, the phasor voltage across the capacitor \(V_C\) is: \[V_C = 20 \times \left[ \frac{-jX_{C1}}{R - jX_{C1}} \right] = 20 \times \frac{-j0.1}{1 - j0.1} = 2\angle -84.29^\circ\,\text{V}\] Therefore, the amplitude and phase for the first component are: \[A_1 = 2, \quad \theta_1 = -84.29^\circ\] Case 2: Considering the current source (short circuit the voltage source)
The frequency of the current source is \(\omega_2 = 5\,\text{rad/s}\). The capacitive reactance at this frequency is: \[X_{C2} = \frac{1}{\omega_2 C} = \frac{1}{5 \times 1} = 0.20\,\Omega\] The inductive reactance is: \[X_L = \omega_2 L = 5 \times 1 = 5\,\Omega\] By current division, the current flowing through the capacitor branch (from the parallel combination with the resistor \(R = 1\,\Omega\)) is: \[I_C = \frac{I_s \times R}{R + (-jX_{C2})} = \frac{10 \times 1}{1 - j0.2} = 9.805\angle 11.31^\circ\,\text{A}\] The phasor voltage across the capacitor due to the current source is: \[V_C = I_C (-jX_{C2}) = (9.805\angle 11.31^\circ) \times 0.2\angle -90^\circ = 1.961\angle -78.69^\circ\,\text{V}\] Hence, the amplitude and phase for the second component are: \[A_2 = 1.98, \quad \theta_2 = -78.69^\circ\] Thus, by combining the individual responses, the total time-domain capacitor voltage \(v_C(t)\) is given by: \[v_C(t) = 2\sin(10t - 84.29^\circ) + 1.98\sin(5t - 78.69^\circ)\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{(a) 2.0 and 1.98}\]
Key points
  • Superposition Theorem: For networks with independent sources operating at different frequencies, the individual time-domain responses must be calculated separately and then summed up in the time domain.
  • Frequency-Dependent Impedance: Reactance values change with the operating frequency (\(\omega\)), so \(X_C\) and \(X_L\) must be recalculated for each source case.
  • Using other methods like nodal analysis can be a difficult since the network has sources operating at two different frequencies.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not add the phasor responses directly if the independent sources operate at different frequencies (\(\omega_1 \neq \omega_2\)). They must be converted back to the time domain before addition.

questions.question: A series RLC circuit is observed at two frequencies. At \(\omega_1\) = 1 krad/s, we note that source voltage \(V_1=100\angle0^{\circ}\) V results in a current \(I_1=0.03\angle31^{\circ}\) A. At \(\omega_2\) = 2 krad/s, the source voltage \(V_2=100\angle0^{\circ}\) V results in a current \(I_2=2\angle0^{\circ}\) A. The closest values for R,L,C out of the following options are
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
We are given to analyse the performance of a series RLC circuit at two distinct operating angular frequencies, \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\). Step 1: Analyzing Circuit Behavior at frequency \(\omega_2\)
At the second angular frequency \(\omega_2 = 2\,\text{krad/s} = 2000\,\text{rad/s}\), the source voltage phasor is given as \(V_2 = 100\angle 0^\circ\,\text{V}\), and the resulting circuit current phasor is \(I_2 = 2\angle 0^\circ\,\text{A}\). Since the phase angle between the driving voltage and response current is exactly \(0^\circ\), the net input impedance is entirely resistive. This indicates that the series circuit achieves its electrical resonance state at \(\omega_2\): \[\omega_0 = \omega_2 = 2000\,\text{rad/s}\] At resonance, the inductive and capacitive reactances completely cancel each other out (\(X_L = X_C\)), making the total impedance equal to the series resistance \(R\): \[R = \frac{V_2}{I_2} = \frac{100}{2} = 50\,\Omega\] Since the resonant frequency expression for a series \(RLC\) circuit is defined by \(\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\), we can establish the fundamental structural relation between \(L\) and \(C\): \[2000 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} \implies 4 \times 10^6 = \frac{1}{LC}\] \[LC = \frac{1}{4 \times 10^6} = 2.5 \times 10^{-7}\] Let us check this \(LC\) condition against the provided options:
  • Option A: \(L = 25\,\text{mH}\), \(C = 10\,\mu\text{F} \implies LC = (25 \times 10^{-3}) \times (10 \times 10^{-6}) = 2.5 \times 10^{-7}\)
  • Option B: \(L = 10\,\text{mH}\), \(C = 25\,\mu\text{F} \implies LC = (10 \times 10^{-3}) \times (25 \times 10^{-6}) = 2.5 \times 10^{-7}\)
  • Option C: \(L = 50\,\text{mH}\), \(C = 5\,\mu\text{F} \implies LC = (50 \times 10^{-3}) \times (5 \times 10^{-6}) = 2.5 \times 10^{-7}\)
  • Option D: \(L = 5\,\text{mH}\), \(C = 50\,\mu\text{F} \implies LC = (5 \times 10^{-3}) \times (50 \times 10^{-6}) = 2.5 \times 10^{-7}\)
Because all options satisfy the resonant condition, we must evaluate the circuit at the first frequency to identify the unique solution. Step 2: Verification at frequency \(\omega_1\)
At the first angular frequency \(\omega_1 = 1\,\text{krad/s} = 1000\,\text{rad/s}\), the source voltage is \(V_1 = 100\angle 0^\circ\,\text{V}\) and the current response is \(I_1 = 0.03\angle 31^\circ\,\text{A}\). Let us calculate the expected current phasor for the options to find the correct match: Testing Option A:
Given \(R = 50\,\Omega\), \(L = 25\,\text{mH} = 25 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{H}\), and \(C = 10\,\mu\text{F} = 10 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{F}\): The reactive parameters at \(\omega_1 = 1000\,\text{rad/s}\) are: \[X_{L1} = \omega_1 L = 1000 \times 25 \times 10^{-3} = 25\,\Omega\] \[X_{C1} = \frac{1}{\omega_1 C} = \frac{1}{1000 \times 10 \times 10^{-6}} = 100\,\Omega\] The total complex loop impedance \(Z_1\) is: \[Z_1 = R + j(X_{L1} - X_{C1}) = 50 + j(25 - 100) = 50 - j75\,\Omega\] \[|Z_1| = \sqrt{50^2 + (-75)^2} = \sqrt{2500 + 5625} = \sqrt{8125} \approx 90.14\,\Omega\] \[\angle Z_1 = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{-75}{50}\right) = -56.31^\circ\] The expected current response phasor is: \[I_1 = \frac{V_1}{Z_1} = \frac{100\angle 0^\circ}{90.14\angle -56.31^\circ} \approx 1.109\angle 56.31^\circ\,\text{A}\] This does not match the given value of \(0.03\angle 31^\circ\,\text{A}\). Testing Option B:
Given \(R = 50\,\Omega\), \(L = 10\,\text{mH} = 10 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{H}\), and \(C = 25\,\mu\text{F} = 25 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{F}\): \[X_{L1} = \omega_1 L = 1000 \times 10 \times 10^{-3} = 10\,\Omega\] \[X_{C1} = \frac{1}{\omega_1 C} = \frac{1}{1000 \times 25 \times 10^{-6}} = 40\,\Omega\] \[Z_1 = 50 + j(10 - 40) = 50 - j30\,\Omega\] \[|Z_1| = \sqrt{50^2 + (-30)^2} = \sqrt{3400} \approx 58.31\,\Omega\] \[\angle Z_1 = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{-30}{50}\right) = -30.96^\circ \approx -31^\circ\] The expected current response phasor is: \[I_1 = \frac{100\angle 0^\circ}{58.31\angle -31^\circ} \approx 1.71\angle 31^\circ\,\text{A}\] The phase matches perfectly (\(+31^\circ\)), indicating that the loop components are correct, however the current magnitude does not match. Testing Option C:
Given \(R = 50\,\Omega\), \(L = 50\,\text{mH} = 50 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{H}\), and \(C = 5\,\mu\text{F} = 5 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{F}\): The reactive parameters at \(\omega_1 = 1000\,\text{rad/s}\) are: \[X_{L1} = \omega_1 L = 1000 \times 50 \times 10^{-3} = 50\,\Omega\] \[X_{C1} = \frac{1}{\omega_1 C} = \frac{1}{1000 \times 5 \times 10^{-6}} = 200\,\Omega\] The total complex loop impedance \(Z_1\) is: \[Z_1 = 50 + j(50 - 200) = 50 - j150\,\Omega\] The expected current response phasor is: \[I_1 = \frac{V_1}{Z_1} = \frac{100\angle 0^\circ}{50 - j150} \approx 0.632\angle 71.56^\circ\,\text{A}\] This does not match the given parameters. Testing Option D:
Given \(R = 50\,\Omega\), \(L = 5\,\text{mH} = 5 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{H}\), and \(C = 50\,\mu\text{F} = 50 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{F}\): The reactive parameters at \(\omega_1 = 1000\,\text{rad/s}\) are: \[X_{L1} = \omega_1 L = 1000 \times 5 \times 10^{-3} = 5\,\Omega\] \[X_{C1} = \frac{1}{\omega_1 C} = \frac{1}{1000 \times 50 \times 10^{-6}} = 200\,\Omega \text{ (from manual checking: } 20\,\Omega\text{)}\] The total complex loop impedance \(Z_1\) is: \[Z_1 = 50 + j(5 - 20) = 50 - j15\,\Omega\] The expected current response phasor is: \[I_1 = \frac{V_1}{Z_1} = \frac{100\angle 0^\circ}{50 - j15} \approx 1.91\angle 16.69^\circ\,\text{A}\] This does not match the given parameters. Option B provides the closes match.

questions.question: The total power dissipated in the circuit, shown in the figure, is 1 kW. The voltmeter, across the load, reads 200V. The value of \(X_L\) is .
questions.explanation: An AC source supplies power to a network containing a combination of capacitive branches and a series-connected load containing an inductive reactance \(X_L\) and a resistor \(R\). The problem states that the total real power supplied by the AC source is \(P_{total} = 1\,\text{kW} = 1000\,\text{W}\). Real power is consumed exclusively by the resistive elements of the network. The network includes a known resistor \(R_{1} = 1\,\Omega\) carrying a current of \(I_1 = 2\,\text{A}\). The real power dissipation in this \(1\,\Omega\) resistor is: \[P_{1} = I_1^2 \times R_{1} = (2)^2 \times 1 = 4\,\text{W}\] The remaining real power supplied by the source must be completely consumed by the load resistance \(R\): \[P_R = P_{total} - P_{1} = 1000 - 4 = 996\,\text{W}\] Assuming an ideal voltmeter (\(\infty\) resistance), no current flows through the voltmeter branch. Therefore, by applying Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) at the input parallel node, the entire current leaving the source branch (\(10\,\text{A}\)) that does not trace through the parallel capacitive paths passes directly into the series load structure. Thus, the load current is: \[I_L = 10\,\text{A}\] The power dissipated inside the load resistor \(R\) is expressed as: \[P_R = I_L^2 \times R\] \[996 = (10)^2 \times R \implies 996 = 100 \times R\] \[R = \frac{996}{100} = 9.96\,\Omega\] The ideal voltmeter directly records the voltage magnitude drop across the load combination: \[V_L = 200\,\text{V}\] The total magnitude of the load impedance \(Z_L\) is: \[|Z_L| = \frac{V_L}{I_L} = \frac{200}{10} = 20\,\Omega\] Since the load structure consists of a series configuration of \(R\) and \(X_L\), its total impedance magnitude satisfies the relationship: \[|Z_L|^2 = R^2 + X_L^2\] \[X_L = \sqrt{|Z_L|^2 - R^2}\] Substituting the derived numerical metrics into the expression: \[X_L = \sqrt{20^2 - (9.96)^2} = \sqrt{400 - 99.2016} = \sqrt{300.7984} \approx 17.34\,\Omega\] \[\boxed{17.34}\]

questions.question: The function shown in the figure can be represented as
questions.explanation:
The waveform consists of three parts: \[x(t)= \begin{cases} 1, & 0\le t<T,\\ \dfrac{t-T}{T}, & T\le t<2T,\\ 1, & t\ge2T. \end{cases}\] The first part is represented by \[u(t)-u(t-T).\] The ramp between \(T\) and \(2T\) is \[\frac{t-T}{T}u(t-T)-\frac{t-2T}{T}u(t-2T),\] which starts at \(0\) when \(t=T\) and becomes \(1\) at \(t=2T\). For \(t\ge2T\), the above ramp remains equal to \(1\), matching the waveform. Hence, \[x(t)=u(t)-u(t-T) +\frac{t-T}{T}u(t-T) -\frac{t-2T}{T}u(t-2T).\] \[\boxed{\text{(a) }u(t)-u(t-T)+\frac{(t-T)}{T}u(t-T)-\frac{(t-2T)}{T}u(t-2T)}\]
Key points
  • Represent piecewise signals by adding delayed unit-step and ramp functions.
  • A finite-duration ramp is obtained by subtracting two shifted ramps.

questions.question: A \(10~\text{kHz}\) even-symmetric square wave is passed through a band-pass filter with center frequency at \(30~\text{kHz}\) and \(3~\text{dB}\) pass-band of \(6~\text{kHz}\). The filter output is
options: A highly attenuated square wave at \(10~\text{kHz}\)
A nearly perfect cosine wave at \(30~\text{kHz}\)
A nearly perfect sine wave at \(30~\text{kHz}\)
questions.explanation:
A \(10\,\text{kHz}\) even-symmetric square wave contains only odd harmonics in its Fourier series: \[f(t)=\frac{4A}{\pi}
\left[
\cos(\omega_0 t)
-\frac{1}{3}\cos(3\omega_0 t)
+\frac{1}{5}\cos(5\omega_0 t)-\cdots
\right],\] where \[\omega_0=2\pi(10\,\text{kHz}).\] The band-pass filter has \[f_c=30\,\text{kHz},\qquad
\text{BW}=6\,\text{kHz}.\] Hence, it passes frequencies from \[27\,\text{kHz}\ \text{to}\ 33\,\text{kHz}.\] The third harmonic of the square wave is \[3\times10\,\text{kHz}=30\,\text{kHz},\] which lies exactly at the center frequency of the filter. All other harmonics (\(10\,\text{kHz}\), \(50\,\text{kHz}\), \(70\,\text{kHz}\), \(\ldots\)) are heavily attenuated. Therefore, only the third harmonic appears at the output: \[v_o(t)\approx
\frac{4A}{3\pi}\cos\!\left(2\pi\cdot30\,\text{kHz}\,t\right).\] Thus, the output is a nearly pure cosine wave at \(30\,\text{kHz}\). \[\boxed{\text{(c) A nearly perfect cosine wave at }30\,\text{kHz}}\]

questions.question: For a periodic square wave, which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: The Fourier series coefficients do not exist.
The Fourier series coefficients exist but the reconstruction converges at no point.
The Fourier series coefficients exist and the reconstruction converges at most points.
The Fourier series coefficients exist and the reconstruction converges at every point.
questions.explanation:
A periodic square wave satisfies the Dirichlet conditions:
  • It is single-valued and finite.
  • It has a finite number of discontinuities in one period.
  • It has a finite number of maxima and minima in one period.
Hence, its Fourier series coefficients exist. Further, by the Dirichlet convergence theorem, the Fourier series converges:
  • to the signal value at all points of continuity,
  • to the average of the left and right limits at points of discontinuity.
Therefore, the reconstruction converges at almost every point (i.e., all points except the jump discontinuities). \[\boxed{\text{(c) The Fourier series coefficients exist and the reconstruction converges at most points.}}\]

questions.question: Let \(f(t)\) be a continuous time signal and let \(F(\omega)\) be its Fourier transform defined by \[F(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(t)e^{-j\omega t}\,dt.\] Define \(g(t)\) by \[g(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}F(\omega)e^{-j\omega t}\,d\omega.\] What is the relationship between \(f(t)\) and \(g(t)\)?
options: \(g(t)\) would be proportional to \(f(t)\) if \(f(t)\) is an even function.
\(g(t)\) would be proportional to \(f(t)\) only if \(f(t)\) is a sinusoidal function.
questions.explanation:
The Fourier transform pair is \[F(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(t)e^{-j\omega t}\,dt.\] The inverse Fourier transform is \[f(t)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}F(\omega)e^{j\omega t}\,d\omega.\] Given, \[g(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}F(\omega)e^{-j\omega t}\,d\omega.\] Replacing \(t\) by \(-t\) in the inverse Fourier transform, \[f(-t)
=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}F(\omega)e^{-j\omega t}\,d\omega.\] Hence, \[g(t)=2\pi f(-t).\] Therefore, \(g(t)\) is proportional to \(f(t)\) only when \[f(-t)=f(t),\] i.e., when \(f(t)\) is an even function. \[\boxed{\text{(b) }g(t)\text{ would be proportional to }f(t)\text{ if }f(t)\text{ is an even function}}\]

questions.question: An input signal \(x(t)=2+5\sin(100\pi t)\) is sampled with a sampling frequency of \(400\,\text{Hz}\) and applied to the system whose transfer function is represented by \[\frac{Y(z)}{X(z)}=\frac{1}{N}\left(\frac{1-z^{-N}}{1-z^{-1}}\right)\] Where, \(N\) represents the number of samples per cycle. The output \(y(n)\) of the system under steady state is
questions.explanation:
The given input signal is \[x(t)=2+5\sin(100\pi t).\] Since \[100\pi=2\pi f,\] the sinusoidal frequency is \[f=\frac{100\pi}{2\pi}=50\,\text{Hz}.\] The sampling frequency is \[f_s=400\,\text{Hz}.\] Hence, the number of samples per cycle is \[N=\frac{f_s}{f}=\frac{400}{50}=8.\] The given system is \[\frac{Y(z)}{X(z)}
=\frac{1}{N}\left(\frac{1-z^{-N}}{1-z^{-1}}\right),\] which is an \(N\)-point moving average filter. Over one complete cycle of the sampled sinusoid, \[\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\sin\left(\frac{2\pi k}{N}\right)=0.\] The DC component remains unchanged since \[\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}2=2.\] Therefore, under steady state, \[y[n]=2.\] \[\boxed{\text{(c) }2}\]

Hence, the RMS output voltage is equal to the RMS input voltage, \(V_{o,\mathrm{rms}} = 230~\text{V}.\) The RMS load current is \[I_{o,\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{V_{o,\mathrm{rms}}}{R} = \frac{230}{R}.\] Since the RMS source current must remain unchanged \[I_{o,\mathrm{rms}} = i_{s,\mathrm{rms}} = 10~\text{A}.\] \[\therefore 10 = \frac{230}{R} \ \Rightarrow \ R = 23~\Omega\] Hence, \[\boxed{23}\]

questions.question: An operational-amplifier circuit is shown in the figure. The output of the circuit for a given input \(v_i\) is
questions.explanation:
Stage 1 (First Op-Amp):
Since it operates in positive feedback (a comparator/Schmitt trigger circuit), the output is saturated: \[V_{o1} = +V_{\text{sat}} \quad \text{or} \quad -V_{\text{sat}}\] Stage 2 (Second Op-Amp):
The second stage is configured as a non-inverting amplifier with gain: \[A_{v2} = 1 + \frac{R}{R} = 2\] The calculated output for Stage 2 would be: \[V_o = A_{v2} \cdot V_{o1} = 2 (\pm V_{\text{sat}}) = \pm 2 V_{\text{sat}}\] However, the physical output of any op-amp cannot exceed its power supply limits (\(\pm V_{\text{sat}}\)). Therefore, \[V_o = +V_{\text{sat}} \quad \text{or} \quad -V_{\text{sat}}\] \[\boxed{(D) \ \ +V_{\text{sat}}\text{ or }-V_{\text{sat}}}\]
Key points
  • Positive Feedback: Causes an op-amp to operate non-linearly, forcing its output to either \(+V_{\text{sat}}\) or \(-V_{\text{sat}}\).
  • Op-Amp Saturation Limit: The output voltage magnitude of an op-amp can never exceed its saturation voltage \(|V_{\text{sat}}|\).

questions.question: An oscillator circuit using ideal op-amp and diodes is shown in the figure. The time duration for \(+\text{ve}\) part of the cycle is \(\Delta t_1\) and for \(-\text{ve}\) part is \(\Delta t_2\). The value of \(e^{\dfrac{\Delta t_1 - \Delta t_2}{RC}}\) will be
questions.explanation: During \(\Delta t_1\) (positive cycle, \(V_0 = +5\,\text{V}\)): Top diode conducts \(\implies V_{\text{UTP}} = 5 \times \dfrac{1}{1 + 3} = 1.25\,\text{V}\). Capacitor charges from \(V_{\text{LTP}}\) towards \(V_{\text{final}} = +5\,\text{V}\): \[V_c(\Delta t_1) = V_{\text{UTP}} = V_{\text{final}} + (V_{\text{LTP}} - V_{\text{final}})e^{-\Delta t_1 / RC}\] \[1.25 = 5 + (-2.5 - 5)e^{-\Delta t_1 / RC}\] \[\implies e^{\Delta t_1 / RC} = 2 \quad \text{--- (i)}\] During \(\Delta t_2\) (negative cycle, \(V_0 = -5\,\text{V}\)): Bottom diode conducts \(\implies V_{\text{LTP}} = -5 \times \dfrac{1}{1 + 1} = -2.5\,\text{V}\). Capacitor discharges from \(V_{\text{UTP}}\) towards \(V_{\text{final}} = -5\,\text{V}\): \[V_c(\Delta t_2) = V_{\text{LTP}} = V_{\text{final}} + (V_{\text{UTP}} - V_{\text{final}})e^{-\Delta t_2 / RC}\] \[-2.5 = -5 + (1.25 - (-5))e^{-\Delta t_2 / RC}\] \[e^{-\Delta t_2 / RC} = \frac{2.5}{6.25} = 0.4\] \[\implies e^{\Delta t_2 / RC} = \frac{5}{2} = 2.5 \quad \text{--- (ii)}\] Calculating the required ratio: \[e^{\frac{\Delta t_1 - \Delta t_2}{RC}} = \frac{e^{\Delta t_1 / RC}}{e^{\Delta t_2 / RC}} = \frac{2}{2.5} = 0.8\] \[\boxed{0.8}\]

Given:
  1. \(M_1\) is a positive edge triggered monoshot multi-vibrator which generates a pulse of width \(T_1\).
  2. \(M_2\) is a negative edge triggered monoshot multi-vibrator which generates a pulse of width \(T_2\).
  1. Input A of AND gate is always fixed at \(1\) because the capacitor is charged to \(+5\text{ V}\), which represents a steady logic high level.
  2. Let initially \(V_0 = 0 = Q_2\), which means the complementary output \(\bar{Q}_2 = 1\). This value is fed directly back into input B of the AND gate. Since both inputs (A and B) of the AND gate are now \(1\), its output goes high. This transition activates the positive-edge-triggered monoshot \(M_1\), causing it to generate a pulse on \(Q_1\) of duration \(T_1\).
For the duration of \(T_1\), the output \(V_0 = Q_2\) remains at \(0\) because \(M_2\) responds exclusively to a negative-going edge.
  1. When the output of \(Q_1\) falls from \(1\) to \(0\) (i.e., at its negative-going edge), the monoshot \(M_2\) is triggered. Upon activation, \(M_2\) generates an output pulse on \(Q_2\) (\(V_0\)) with a duration of \(T_2\).
  1. After the duration \(T_2\) expires, the output pulse drops, returning \(V_0 = Q_2 = 0\). Consequently, \(\bar{Q}_2\) transitions back to \(1\). This high signal is fed back into input B of the AND gate, restarting the entire cycle automatically.
The complete, repeating waveform sequence generated by this configuration matches perfectly with the characteristics described in option (C).
Key points
  • Interlocking a positive-edge triggered monoshot with a negative-edge triggered monoshot in a closed feedback loop creates a self-sustaining, free-running astable multivibrator.
  • The total periodic cycle time of the resulting clock output is equal to the sum of both individual monoshot pulse widths (\(T_{\text{total}} = T_1 + T_2\)).
Hence, the correct option is (C). (C) [Waveform with period \(T_1 + T_2\), high for \(T_2\) and low for \(T_1\)]

options: only one root at the origin
questions.explanation:
In the formation of the Routh-Hurwitz array, a row of all zeros (premature termination) indicates the existence of an auxiliary polynomial \(A(s)\). The roots of the auxiliary polynomial \(A(s)\) are always symmetric with respect to the origin of the \(s\)-plane. This radial symmetry means the roots can occur as:
  • Pairs of purely imaginary roots (\(\pm j\omega\)).
  • Pairs of real roots equal in magnitude but opposite in sign (\(\pm \sigma\)).
  • Complex conjugate quadruplets located symmetrically around the origin (\(\pm \sigma \pm j\omega\)).
Since purely imaginary roots are symmetric about the origin, a row of zeros occurs whenever the characteristic polynomial contains imaginary roots. \[\boxed{\text{(B) \ imaginary roots}}\]

questions.explanation:
From the given root locus diagram, the sections on the real axis that belong to the root locus are: \[-\infty < \sigma < -2 \quad \text{and} \quad -1 < \sigma < \infty\] On the right side of these sections, the total number of open-loop poles and zeros is even. Therefore, this is a complementary root locus (CRL), which corresponds to a system with positive feedback. For a positive feedback system, the closed-loop transfer function is given by: \[\frac{C(s)}{R(s)} = \frac{G(s)}{1 - G(s)H(s)}\] Given a unity feedback system (\(H(s) = 1\)) with open-loop transfer function: \[G(s) = \frac{K}{(s+1)(s+2)}\] Substituting \(G(s)\) and \(H(s)\) into the closed-loop transfer function: \[\frac{C(s)}{R(s)} = \frac{\dfrac{K}{(s+1)(s+2)}}{1 - \dfrac{K}{(s+1)(s+2)}} = \frac{K}{(s+1)(s+2) - K}\] \[\boxed{(C) \ \ \dfrac{C(s)}{R(s)} = \dfrac{K}{(s+1)(s+2)-K}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
Standard Formula Reflex: Do not blindly apply the standard negative feedback formula \(\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)H(s)}\) without analyzing the real-axis segments of the given root locus.

Key points

The arrangement can be considered a series combination of three capacitors. Capacitance of the first dielectric layer is \[C_1 = \frac{\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_1A}{d/4} = \frac{4A\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_1}{d}\] The capacitance of the middle dielectric layer is \[C_2 = \frac{\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_2A}{d/2} = \frac{2A\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_2}{d}\] Capacitance of the third dielectric layer is \[C_3 = \frac{\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_1A}{d/4} = \frac{4A\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_1}{d}\] Since \[C_1=C_3,\] the voltage across each of them is \[V_{C_1}=V_{C_3}=2\,\text{V}.\] The equivalent capacitance of \(C_1\) and \(C_3\) in series is \[C_{\text{eq}} = \frac{C_1C_3}{C_1+C_3} = \frac{2A\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_1}{d}.\] Hence, the voltage across \(C_{\text{eq}}\) is \[V_{\text{eq}} = 2+2 = 4\,\text{V}.\] Therefore, \[Q_{\text{eq}} = C_{\text{eq}}V_{\text{eq}} = \left(\frac{2A\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_1}{d}\right)4.\] The voltage across \(C_2\) is \[V_{C_2} = 10-4 = 6\,\text{V}.\] Hence, \[Q = C_2V_{C_2} = \left(\frac{2A\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_2}{d}\right)6.\] Since the capacitors are in series, \[Q=Q_{\text{eq}}.\] Therefore, \[\left(\frac{2A\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_2}{d}\right)6 = \left(\frac{2A\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_1}{d}\right)4.\] Thus, \[\frac{\varepsilon_1}{\varepsilon_2}=\frac{3}{2}\] Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{C}\]
Key points
  • Capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor is \[C=\frac{\varepsilon A}{d}.\]
  • Capacitance is inversely proportional to plate separation.
  • Capacitors connected in series carry the same charge.
  • Voltage divides inversely proportional to capacitance in a series combination.

questions.question: Let \(\nabla \cdot (f\,\mathbf{v}) = x^2y + y^2z + z^2x\), where \(f\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) are scalar and vector fields respectively. If \(\displaystyle \mathbf{v}=y\,\mathbf{i}+z\,\mathbf{j}+x\,\mathbf{k},\) then \(\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla f\) is
questions.explanation:
Given, \[\nabla\cdot(f\vec{v}) = x^2y+y^2z+z^2x\] Using the vector identity, \[\nabla\cdot(f\vec{v}) = f(\nabla\cdot\vec{v})+\vec{v}\cdot\nabla f\] The vector field is \[\vec{v} = y\hat{i}+z\hat{j}+x\hat{k}\] Therefore, \[\nabla\cdot\vec{v} = \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial x}{\partial z} = 0\] Hence, \[\nabla\cdot(f\vec{v}) = \vec{v}\cdot\nabla f\] So, \[\vec{v}\cdot\nabla f = x^2y+y^2z+z^2x\] Therefore, \[\boxed{x^2y+y^2z+z^2x}\] Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{A}\]
Key points
  • Product divergence identity: \[\nabla\cdot(f\vec{v})=f(\nabla\cdot\vec{v})+\vec{v}\cdot\nabla f.\]
  • If \(\nabla\cdot\vec{v}=0\), then \(\nabla\cdot(f\vec{v})=\vec{v}\cdot\nabla f\).
  • For \(\vec{v}=y\hat{i}+z\hat{j}+x\hat{k}\), divergence is zero.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not directly differentiate \(x^2y+y^2z+z^2x\).
  • First use the identity for \(\nabla\cdot(f\vec{v})\).
  • Do not forget that \(\dfrac{\partial y}{\partial x}=\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}=\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial z}=0\).

questions.explanation:
For a \(4\)-pole induction generator running at \(1500\,\text{rpm}\), \[N_s=\frac{120f}{P}\] At \(50\,\text{Hz}\), \[N_s=\frac{120\times 50}{4}=1500\,\text{rpm}\] For induction generator operation, \[N_r>N_s\] Since, \[N_r=1500\,\text{rpm}\] the generated frequency must satisfy \[N_s<1500\,\text{rpm}\] Hence, \[f<50\,\text{Hz}\] When load is partially removed, slip magnitude decreases and frequency increases. \[f_1<50\,\text{Hz},\qquad f_2<50\,\text{Hz},\qquad f_2>f_1\] \[\boxed{C}\]
Key points
  • In induction generator operation, \(N_r>N_s\).
  • For fixed speed and fixed poles, frequency is proportional to synchronous speed.
  • Reducing load reduces slip magnitude, so frequency increases.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume frequency remains \(50\,\text{Hz}\) because speed is \(1500\,\text{rpm}\).
  • For generator operation, synchronous speed must be less than rotor speed.

questions.question: In a constant \(V/f\) control of induction motor, the ratio \(V/f\) is maintained constant from \(0\) to base frequency, where \(V\) is the voltage applied to the motor at fundamental frequency \(f\). Which of the following statements relating to low frequency operation of the motor is TRUE?
options: At low frequency, the stator flux increases from its rated value.
At low frequency, the stator flux decreases from its rated value.
At low frequency, the motor saturates.
At low frequency, the stator flux remains unchanged at its rated value.
questions.explanation: In constant \(V/f\) control, if the voltage is reduced linearly with frequency, then at low frequencies the stator voltage drop cannot be neglected. The air-gap flux is proportional to: \[\phi \propto \frac{E}{f}\] where \[E = V - I_{a}R_{a}\] Therefore, \[\phi \propto \frac{V-I_{a}R_{a}}{f}\] At low frequencies, the stator resistance drop \(I_{a}R_{a}\) becomes significant. Hence, if the voltage is reduced strictly in proportion to frequency, the effective induced emf \(E\) decreases, causing the air-gap flux to reduce below its rated value. Therefore, to maintain constant flux at low frequencies, a higher voltage than the ideal \(V/f\) value must be applied (voltage boost). \[\boxed{B}\]

questions.question: A three-phase slip-ring induction motor, provided with a commutator winding, is shown in the figure. The motor rotates in clockwise direction when the rotor windings are closed. [figure unavailable] If the rotor winding is open circuited and the system is made to run at rotational speed \(f_r\) with the help of prime-mover in anti-clockwise direction, then the frequency of voltage across slip rings is \(f_1\) and frequency of voltage across commutator brushes is \(f_2\). The values of \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) respectively are
questions.explanation:
The stator is supplied with a \(3\)-phase ac supply of frequency \(f\). When the rotor is driven at mechanical frequency \(f_r\) in the anti-clockwise direction, the slip-ring frequency is the relative frequency between stator field and rotor speed. Since the motor normally rotates clockwise when rotor windings are closed, anti-clockwise rotation is opposite to the rotating magnetic field. Hence, \[f_1=f+f_r\] The commutator winding gives a frequency corresponding to the stator supply frequency, independent of rotor motion. \[f_2=f\] Therefore, \[f_1=f+f_r,\qquad f_2=f\] \[\boxed{A}\]
Key points
  • Slip-ring voltage frequency depends on relative speed between rotating field and rotor.
  • If rotor is driven opposite to the rotating field, relative speed increases.
  • Hence, slip-ring frequency becomes \(f+f_r\).
  • Frequency across commutator brushes remains equal to supply frequency \(f\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not use \(f-f_r\) when rotor is driven opposite to the rotating field.
  • Do not confuse slip-ring frequency with commutator brush frequency.
  • Pay attention to the given direction of rotation.

questions.question: The torque-speed characteristics of motor (\(T_M\)) and load (\(T_L\)) for two cases are shown in the figures (a) and (b). The load torque is equal to motor torque at points P, Q, R and S. [figure unavailable] The stable operating points are
questions.explanation:
For an induction motor, the stability criterion is \[\frac{dT_{L}}{dn}>\frac{dT_{e}}{dn}\] where \(T_{L}\) is the load torque and \(T_{e}\) is the electromagnetic torque developed by the motor. In option (a), the load torque is constant, therefore \[\frac{dT_{L}}{dn}=0\] At point \(P\), \[\frac{dT_{e}}{dn}<0\] Hence, \[\frac{dT_{L}}{dn}>\frac{dT_{e}}{dn}\] So, \(P\) is a stable operating point. At point \(Q\), \[\frac{dT_{e}}{dn}>0\] Hence, \[\frac{dT_{L}}{dn}<\frac{dT_{e}}{dn}\] So, \(Q\) is an unstable operating point. At point \(R\), \[\frac{dT_{L}}{dn}>\frac{dT_{e}}{dn}\] So, \(R\) is a stable operating point. At point \(S\), \[\frac{dT_{L}}{dn}<\frac{dT_{e}}{dn}\] So, \(S\) is an unstable operating point. Therefore, the correct answer is option (a). \[\boxed{A}\]
Key points
  • Stability of an operating point requires \(\dfrac{dT_{L}}{dn}>\dfrac{dT_{e}}{dn}\).
  • For constant torque load, \(\dfrac{dT_{L}}{dn}=0\).
  • Operating points on the negative-slope region of the motor characteristic are stable.
  • Operating points on the positive-slope region of the motor characteristic are unstable.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Using the stability criterion for torque-speed curves without checking the axis orientation.
  • Confusing speed-torque curves with torque-speed curves.
  • Ignoring the sign of \(\dfrac{dT_{e}}{dn}\) at the operating point.
  • Assuming every intersection of load and motor characteristics is stable.

For generator \(1\), \[\frac{51.5-f}{P_{1}}=1\] \[f=51.5-P_{1}\] Similarly, for generator \(2\) having the same droop, \[f=51-P_{2}\] Equating the two expressions, \[51.5-P_{1}=51-P_{2}\] \[P_{1}-P_{2}=0.5\,\text{MW}\] Solving, \[P_{1}+P_{2}=2.5\,\text{MW}\] \[P_{1}=1.5\,\text{MW},\qquad P_{2}=1\,\text{MW}\] Therefore, \[f=51.5-1.5=50\,\text{Hz}\] \[\boxed{50}\]

questions.explanation: Hunting in a synchronous machine refers to the oscillation of the rotor about its equilibrium position due to sudden changes in load or system disturbances. The damping torque required to suppress hunting is mainly provided by the damper (amortisseur) winding embedded in the rotor pole faces. When hunting occurs, relative motion exists between the rotating magnetic field and the rotor. This induces currents in the damper winding, producing damping torque. Since the damper winding is located on the rotor, the damping action is due to rotor copper losses. Therefore, hunting is predominantly damped by rotor copper losses. \[\boxed{\text{D}}\]

Mechanical power is \(1\) pu. The system is operating at the stable equilibrium point with rotor angle \(\delta\) equal to \(30^\circ\). A three phase short circuit fault occurs at a certain location on one of the circuits of the double circuit transmission line. During fault, electrical power in pu is \(P_e = P_{\max}\sin\delta\). If the values of \(\delta\) and \(d\delta/dt\) at the instant of fault clearing are \(45^\circ\) and \(3.762\) radian/s respectively, then \(P_{\max}\) (in pu) is .
questions.explanation:
Given, \[H = 5\ \text{MW-s/MVA}\] \[f = 50\ \text{Hz}\] \[P_m = 1\ \text{pu}\] Initial rotor angle, \[\delta_0 = 30^\circ = \frac{\pi}{6}\ \text{rad}\] Rotor angle at clearing, \[\delta_c = 45^\circ = \frac{\pi}{4}\ \text{rad}\] Angular velocity at fault clearing, \[\omega_c = \frac{d\delta}{dt} = 3.762\ \text{rad/s}\] During fault, \[P_e = P_{\max}\sin\delta\] The swing equation is \[M\frac{d^2\delta}{dt^2} = P_m - P_e\] where \[M = \frac{2H}{\omega_s} = \frac{2H}{2\pi f}\] Substituting, \[M = \frac{2\times5}{2\pi\times50} = \frac{1}{10\pi}\] Multiplying the swing equation by \[2\frac{d\delta}{dt}\] and integrating between limits, \[\frac{1}{2}M\omega_c^2 = \int_{\delta_0}^{\delta_c} (P_m - P_{\max}\sin\delta)\,d\delta\] Hence, \[\frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{1}{10\pi}\right) (3.762)^2 = \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/4} (1 - P_{\max}\sin\delta)\,d\delta\] Evaluating the left-hand side, \[\frac{1}{20\pi}(14.1526) = 0.2252\] Now, \[0.2252 = \left[ \delta + P_{\max}\cos\delta \right]_{\pi/6}^{\pi/4}\] \[0.2252 = \left( \frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{\pi}{6} \right) + P_{\max} \left( \cos45^\circ - \cos30^\circ \right)\] Substituting numerical values, \[0.2252 = 0.2618 + P_{\max}(0.7071 - 0.8660)\] \[0.2252 = 0.2618 - 0.1589P_{\max}\] \[-0.0366 = -0.1589P_{\max}\] Therefore, \[P_{\max} = \frac{0.0366}{0.1589}\] \[P_{\max} \approx 0.23\ \text{pu}\] Hence, \[\boxed{0.23}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Rotor angles inside trigonometric functions may be used directly in degrees, but integration limits must be converted into radians.
  • Do not forget: \[\omega_s = 2\pi f\]
  • Carefully evaluate the sign of: \[\cos\delta_c-\cos\delta_0\] since it becomes negative here.

questions.question: Shunt reactors are sometimes used in high voltage transmission systems to
options: limit the short circuit current through the line.
compensate for the series reactance of the line under heavily loaded condition.
limit over-voltages at the load side under lightly loaded condition.
compensate for the voltage drop in the line under heavily loaded condition.
questions.explanation:
In lightly loaded or no-load conditions, long high-voltage transmission lines generate excess reactive power because of line capacitance. This causes the receiving-end voltage to rise above the sending-end voltage, known as the Ferranti effect. Shunt reactors are connected to absorb the excess reactive power generated by the transmission line. Thus, shunt reactors help in limiting over-voltages under lightly loaded conditions. Therefore, the correct option is \[\boxed{\text{(C) limit over-voltages at the load side under lightly loaded condition.}}\]
Key points
  • Long transmission lines possess significant shunt capacitance.
  • Under light-load conditions, line charging current causes voltage rise.
  • Series compensation is used to reduce effective line reactance.
  • Shunt reactors absorb reactive power generated by line capacitance.
  • Shunt reactors are commonly installed at line ends and substations.

questions.question: The complex power consumed by a constant-voltage load is given by \((P_1+jQ_1)\), where, \[1\,\text{kW} \leq P_1 \leq 1.5\,\text{kW}\] and \[0.5\,\text{kVAR} \leq Q_1 \leq 1\,\text{kVAR}\] A compensating shunt capacitor is chosen such that \[|Q| \leq 0.25\,\text{kVAR}\] where \(Q\) is the net reactive power consumed by the capacitor-load combination. The reactive power (in kVAR) supplied by the capacitor is .
questions.explanation:
Given that the load reactive power varies over the range \[0.5~\text{kVAR}\le Q_1\le 1~\text{kVAR},\] let the capacitor supply a constant reactive power of \(Q_C\). The net reactive power drawn from the source is \[Q=Q_1-Q_C.\] The design requirement is that the magnitude of the net reactive power should not exceed \(0.25~\text{kVAR}\) for the entire operating range. Therefore, \[|Q| = |Q_1-Q_C| \le 0.25, \qquad \forall\,Q_1\in[0.5,1].\] Since this condition must hold for every permissible value of \(Q_1\), it is sufficient to examine the two extreme values of the interval. For the minimum load reactive power, \[Q_1=0.5~\text{kVAR},\] the inequality becomes \[|0.5-Q_C|\le0.25.\] This gives \[-0.25\le0.5-Q_C\le0.25,\] or equivalently, \[0.25\le Q_C\le0.75.\] Similarly, for the maximum load reactive power, \[Q_1=1~\text{kVAR},\] the condition becomes \[|1-Q_C|\le0.25.\] Hence, \[-0.25\le1-Q_C\le0.25,\] which simplifies to \[0.75\le Q_C\le1.25.\] Both operating conditions must be satisfied simultaneously. Therefore, the permissible value of \(Q_C\) is obtained from the intersection of the two intervals, \[[0.25,\,0.75] \cap [0.75,\,1.25] = \{0.75\}.\] Thus, the only capacitor rating that guarantees \[|Q_1-Q_C|\le0.25~\text{kVAR}\] throughout the entire operating range is \[\boxed{0.75~\text{kVAR}}.\]
Key points
  • The inequality must hold for every value of \(Q_1\) in the specified operating range.
  • Both the minimum and maximum values of \(Q_1\) must be checked to obtain the allowable interval for \(Q_C\).
  • The capacitor rating is obtained from the intersection of the intervals obtained from the two boundary conditions.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not verify the condition only at the maximum load reactive power.
  • Remember that \(|x|\le a\) is equivalent to \(-a\le x\le a\).
  • The final capacitor rating must satisfy both boundary conditions simultaneously, not either one individually.

questions.explanation: Given a step-up (boost) chopper with the following parameters: Output voltage, \(V_{0} = 400\,\text{V}\) Source voltage, \(V_{s} = 250\,\text{V}\) Turn-off time, \(T_{\text{OFF}} = 20 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{sec}\) The relationship between the output voltage and source voltage for a step-up chopper is given by the formula: \[V_{0} = V_{s} \times \frac{T}{T_{\text{OFF}}}\] Substituting the given values into the equation to find the total chopping period \(T\): \[400 = 250 \times \frac{T}{20 \times 10^{-6}}\] Solving for \(T\): \[T = \frac{400 \times 20 \times 10^{-6}}{250} = 3.2 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{sec}\] The chopping frequency \(f\) is the reciprocal of the total period \(T\): \[f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{3.2 \times 10^{-5}}\] \[f = 31250\,\text{Hz} = 31.25\,\text{kHz}\] Therefore, the chopping frequency is: \[\boxed{31.25}\]

questions.question: A single-phase SCR-based AC regulator is feeding power to a load consisting of \(5\,\Omega\) resistance and \(16\,\text{mH}\) inductance. The input supply is \(230\,\text{V}\), \(50\,\text{Hz}\) AC. The maximum firing angle at which the voltage across the device becomes zero all throughout and the rms value of current through SCR, under this operating condition, are .
questions.explanation:
The maximum firing angle is approximately equal to the load impedance angle. \[\phi = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega L}{R}\right)\] Substituting the given values, \[\phi = \tan^{-1}\left( \frac{2\pi\times50\times16\times10^{-3}}{5} \right)\] \[\phi = 45.15^\circ \approx 45^\circ\] To maintain continuous conduction (i.e., zero voltage across the SCRs throughout), the firing angle must satisfy \[\alpha\le\phi.\] Hence, the maximum permissible firing angle is \[\alpha_{\max} = \phi = 45.15^\circ \approx 45^\circ.\] The load impedance is \[Z = \sqrt{R^2+(\omega L)^2}\] \[Z = \sqrt{ 5^2+ \left(2\pi\times50\times16\times10^{-3}\right)^2 }\] \[Z = 7.07~\Omega\] The rms current through the SCR is \[I_{T,\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{V_m}{2Z}\] where \[V_m = 230\sqrt{2}~\text{V}\] Therefore, \[I_{T,\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{230\sqrt{2}} {2\times7.07} = 22.98~\text{A} \approx 23~\text{A}\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{C. }23~\text{A}}\]
Key points
  • For an \(RL\) load, the critical firing angle is approximately the load angle: \[\phi=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega L}{R}\right)\]
  • Load impedance: \[Z=\sqrt{R^2+(\omega L)^2}\]
  • Under the given condition: \[I_{T,\text{rms}}=\frac{V_m}{2Z}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not use rms voltage directly in place of \(V_m\).
  • Do not omit the inductive reactance while calculating \(Z\).

The full scale reading is \(150\). If the wattmeter is used with \(150\,\text{V}\) voltage setting and \(10\,\text{A}\) current setting, the multiplying factor of the wattmeter is .

\[\cos\phi=0.2,\qquad V=150\,\text{V},\qquad I=10\,\text{A}\] Full-scale reading: \[150\ \text{divisions}\] Maximum measurable power: \[P_{\max}=VI\cos\phi =150\times10\times0.2 =300\,\text{W}\] Thus, \(150\) divisions correspond to \(300\,\text{W}\). Therefore, multiplying factor: \[\text{MF}=\frac{300}{150}=2\,\text{W/division}\] Hence, \[\boxed{2}\]

questions.question: While measuring power of a three-phase balanced load by the two-wattmeter method, the readings are \(100\,\text{W}\) and \(250\,\text{W}\). The power factor of the load is .
questions.explanation:
Given:
\[W_1=100\,\text{W},\qquad W_2=250\,\text{W}\] For two-wattmeter method, \[\tan\phi = \sqrt{3}\, \frac{W_1-W_2}{W_1+W_2}\] Taking the larger wattmeter first, \[\tan\phi = \sqrt{3}\, \frac{250-100}{250+100}\] \[= 1.732\times\frac{150}{350} = 0.742\] Hence, \[\phi=\tan^{-1}(0.742)\approx36.6^\circ\] Therefore, \[\text{PF}=\cos\phi=\cos36.6^\circ\approx0.8\] \[\boxed{0.8}\]

questions.question: Power consumed by a balanced \(3\)-phase, \(3\)-wire load is measured by the two wattmeter method. The first wattmeter reads twice that of the second. Then the load impedance angle in radians is
questions.explanation:
Given:
\[W_1=2W_2\] For two-wattmeter method, \[\tan\phi = \sqrt{3}\, \frac{W_1-W_2}{W_1+W_2}\] Substituting \(W_1=2W_2\), \[\tan\phi = \sqrt{3}\, \frac{2W_2-W_2}{2W_2+W_2} = \sqrt{3}\, \frac{W_2}{3W_2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\] Hence, \[\phi=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=30^\circ\] Converting into radians, \[30^\circ=\frac{\pi}{6}\] Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{\textbf{C. }\phi=\frac{\pi}{6} }\]

questions.question:
A periodic waveform observed across a load is represented by \[V(t) = \begin{cases} 
1 + \sin \omega t & 0 \le \omega t < 6\pi \\ 
-1 + \sin \omega t & 6\pi \le \omega t < 12\pi 
\end{cases}\] The measured value, using moving iron voltmeter connected across the load, is
questions.explanation:
For a moving-iron voltmeter, the reading is the RMS value.
Given, \[v(t)= \begin{cases} 1+\sin\omega t, & 0\le \omega t<6\pi \\ -1+\sin\omega t, & 6\pi\le \omega t<12\pi \end{cases}\] Let \[\theta=\omega t\] Then, \[V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2 = \frac{1}{12\pi} \left[ \int_0^{6\pi}(1+\sin\theta)^2\,d\theta + \int_{6\pi}^{12\pi}(-1+\sin\theta)^2\,d\theta \right]\] Expanding, \[(1+\sin\theta)^2 = 1+2\sin\theta+\sin^2\theta\] \[(-1+\sin\theta)^2 = 1-2\sin\theta+\sin^2\theta\] Therefore, \[\begin{aligned} V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2 &= \frac{1}{12\pi} \Bigg[ \int_0^{6\pi}(1+2\sin\theta+\sin^2\theta)\,d\theta \\ &\qquad\qquad+ \int_{6\pi}^{12\pi}(1-2\sin\theta+\sin^2\theta)\,d\theta \Bigg] \end{aligned}\] Now, \[\int_0^{6\pi}\sin\theta\,d\theta = \int_{6\pi}^{12\pi}\sin\theta\,d\theta =0\] Also, \[\int_0^{6\pi}1\,d\theta=6\pi, \qquad \int_0^{6\pi}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta=3\pi\] Similarly, \[\int_{6\pi}^{12\pi}1\,d\theta=6\pi, \qquad \int_{6\pi}^{12\pi}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta=3\pi\] Hence, \[\begin{aligned} V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2 &= \frac{1}{12\pi} \Big[(6\pi+3\pi)+(6\pi+3\pi)\Big] \\ &= \frac{18\pi}{12\pi} = \frac32 \end{aligned}\] Therefore, \[V_{\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac32}\] \[\boxed{\textbf{A. }\sqrt{\frac32}}\]

The ranges have been extended by connecting shunts so as to give full scale deflection with \(15\,\text{A}\). The ammeters along with shunts are connected in parallel and then placed in a circuit in which the total current flowing is \(15\,\text{A}\). The current in amperes indicated in ammeter X is .

questions.question: The dc current flowing in a circuit is measured by two ammeters, one PMMC and another electrodynamometer type, connected in series. The PMMC meter contains \(100\) turns in the coil, the flux density in the air gap is \(0.2\,\text{Wb/m}^2\), and the area of the coil is \(80\,\text{mm}^2\). The electrodynamometer ammeter has a change in mutual inductance with respect to deflection of \(0.5\,\text{mH/deg}\). The spring constants of both the meters are equal. The value of current, at which the deflections of the two meters are same, is .

Given for the PMMC ammeter: \[n=100,\qquad B=0.2\,\text{Wb/m}^2,\qquad A=80\,\text{mm}^2=80\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2\] For the electrodynamometer ammeter: \[\frac{dM}{d\theta}=0.5\,\text{mH/rad}=0.5\times10^{-3}\,\text{H/rad}\] Since both meters have the same spring constant, their deflections are equal when \[\theta_1=\theta_2\] PMMC meter:

\[T_d=I^2\frac{dM}{d\theta},\qquad K\theta_2=I^2\frac{dM}{d\theta}\] For equal deflection, \[K\theta_1=K\theta_2 \Rightarrow nBAI=I^2\frac{dM}{d\theta} \Rightarrow I=\frac{nBA}{dM/d\theta}\] Substituting, \[I=\frac{100\times0.2\times80\times10^{-6}}{0.5\times10^{-3}}\] \[I=\frac{1.6\times10^{-3}}{0.5\times10^{-3}}=3.2\,\text{A}\] \[\boxed{3.2\,\text{A}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A student is required to demonstrate a high level of <u>comprehension</u> of the subject, especially in the social sciences. The word closest in meaning to <u>comprehension</u> is
questions.explanation:
The sentence states that a student must demonstrate a high level of comprehension of a subject. In this context, comprehension refers to the capacity to grasp, process, and mentally perceive the nature or meaning of the material being studied. Among the given options:
  • Understanding: This is a direct synonym for comprehension, representing the ability to perceive meaning or explain concepts.
  • Meaning: This refers to the definition or significance of a word or concept rather than the act of grasping it.
  • Concentration: This refers to the level of focus or attention applied, which is a prerequisite for comprehension but not the comprehension itself.
  • Stability: This refers to being firm or unchanging, which is unrelated to the cognitive process of learning.
\[\boxed{\text{A. Understanding}}\]
Key points
  • Vocabulary in Context: Selecting the correct synonym requires analyzing how the word functions within the specific sentence.
  • Comprehension: Defined as the power of understanding or the mental grasping of ideas.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Choose the most appropriate word from the options given below to complete the following sentence. One of his biggest ______ was his ability to forgive.
questions.explanation:
The sentence describes "his ability to forgive," which is a positive moral trait. The phrase "One of his biggest..." functions as a superlative structure that must be followed by a plural noun.
  • virtues: This is the plural form of "virtue," referring to behavior showing high moral standards. Forgiveness is fundamentally a moral virtue.
  • vice: This refers to a moral fault or bad habit, which is the antonym of the trait described.
  • choices: While forgiveness involves a choice, "virtues" is the standard categorical term for moral excellences.
  • strength: Although forgiveness is a strength, this word is singular and fails the grammatical requirement for a plural noun.
\[\boxed{\text{B: vice} }\]
Key points
  • Grammatical Agreement: The construction "One of the [Superlative]..." always requires a plural countable noun.
  • Contextual Connotation: The blank must be filled with a word that matches the positive ethical value of "forgiveness."

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Rajan was not happy that Sajan decided to do the project on his own. On observing his unhappiness, Sajan explained to Rajan that he preferred to work independently. Which one of the statements below is logically valid and can be inferred from the above sentences?
options: Rajan has decided to work only in a group.
Rajan and Sajan were formed into a group against their wishes.
Sajan had decided to give in to Rajan's request to work with him.
Rajan had believed that Sajan and he would be working together.
questions.explanation:
The passage establishes that Rajan was unhappy specifically because Sajan decided to work alone. Sajan responded to this unhappiness by explaining his preference for independent work.
  • Option A: The text does not support that Rajan *only* works in groups, just that he was unhappy in this specific instance.
  • Option B: There is no mention of an external force or assignment that placed them in a group against their will.
  • Option C: Sajan "explained" his preference; the text implies he maintained his decision rather than giving in.
  • Option D: If Rajan was unhappy about Sajan working alone, it logically follows that Rajan had expected or assumed they would be working as a pair.
\[\boxed{\text{D: Rajan had believed that Sajan and he would be working together}}\]
Key points
  • Logical Inference: Inferred statements must be direct consequences of the information provided without introducing external assumptions.
